blocks.text: Benzene does undergo addition under forcing conditions. Hydrogenation adds hydrogen to the carbons of the ring; complete hydrogenation gives cyclohexane, a useful solvent and a starting material for other chemicals: C6H6 + 3H2 -> C6H12. Methylbenzene gives methylcyclohexane in the same way.

These reactions destroy the delocalisation of the benzene ring, because the pi electrons are used to form bonds to the new hydrogen atoms. The reactions are exothermic overall, because the new C-H bonds are strong, but they have a high activation barrier. They use the same finely divided nickel catalyst as the hydrogenation of alkenes, at similar temperatures (around 150 C) but at higher pressure.
Chlorine and bromine add in the same way. Without a catalyst, UV light and heat are enough for complete addition: C6H6 + 3Cl2 -> C6H6Cl6 (1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane).

blocks.alt: Top: benzene + 3H2 over nickel at about 150 C and high pressure gives cyclohexane; methylbenzene + 3H2 gives methylcyclohexane. Bottom: benzene + 3Cl2 in UV light and heat gives 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane, a saturated six-carbon ring with one Cl and one H on each carbon.
blocks.caption: Addition of hydrogen and chlorine to benzene (original diagram after the book's equations).
blocks.long_description: In each addition three molecules add across the ring, and the delocalised pi system is lost: the product is a saturated six-membered ring. Hydrogen needs a nickel catalyst and pressure; chlorine needs UV light, which forms chlorine radicals.

blocks.prompt: Predict the product when the trialkylbenzene drawn in Quick Check 20.8 (labelled 3-ethyl-5-propyltoluene) is oxidised with acidified KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7.
blocks.explanation: Every side chain has a benzylic hydrogen, so all three are oxidised to COOH groups: benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylic acid.

blocks.prompt: Predict the product when bromine is added to chlorobenzene in the presence of AlBr3.
blocks.explanation: Ring substitution at the ortho and para positions (Cl is an ortho-para director): mainly 1-bromo-4-chlorobenzene with some 1-bromo-2-chlorobenzene, plus HBr.

blocks.prompt: Predict the product when nitrobenzene is reduced with hydrogen over Ni at high temperature and pressure.
blocks.explanation: The nitro group is reduced to an amino group, giving aniline (phenylamine), C6H5NH2, and water. With enough hydrogen under these forcing conditions the ring can also be hydrogenated, giving cyclohexylamine.

items: C6H6 + 3H2 -> cyclohexane (Ni, about 150 C, high pressure).
Addition destroys the aromatic delocalisation, so it needs harsh conditions.
